scenes.tts: The first film classified bacteria and viruses by what they can do. If both carry genes, why can a bacterium grow while a virus waits? Open them and follow the work.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's color map exactly: bacterium green, virus blue, host pink, genes purple, energy and carbon gold, neutral labels white. A large green bacterium and blue virus fill the frame. Both show purple genes blocks. The green cell pulses; the blue virus stays still. On-screen question: Same genes, different lives?
scenes.narration: The first film classified bacteria and viruses by what they can do. If both carry genes, why can a bacterium grow while a virus waits? Open them and follow the work.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the moving bacterium and virus: Parts Reveal the Difference. Their outlines slowly open without changing position.

scenes.tts: Start with the bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. Its membrane controls what enters and leaves. Cytoplasm fills the inside. Ribosomes build proteins from instructions in D N A. That D N A sits in a nucleoid, a region without a membrane.
scenes.caption: Start with the bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. Its membrane controls what enters and leaves. Cytoplasm fills the inside. Ribosomes build proteins from instructions in DNA. That DNA sits in a nucleoid, a region without a membrane.
scenes.visual: The green bacterium expands to fill most of the frame. Its membrane becomes a thick green boundary. Gold blocks cross through a gate. White ribosome workbenches travel through pale cytoplasm, reading a purple DNA loop in a labeled nucleoid zone. All drawings are labeled schematic.
scenes.narration: Start with the bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. Its membrane controls what enters and leaves. Cytoplasm fills the inside. Ribosomes build proteins from instructions in DNA. That DNA sits in a nucleoid, a region without a membrane.

scenes.tts: Many bacteria also have a cell wall that helps prevent bursting when water enters. Some have a capsule outside. Some have flagella that spin to push them through water. These parts vary, but the working cell remains.
scenes.visual: Water arrows press inward while a tan wall braces the green cell. A translucent capsule appears, then fades to optional. A helical, corkscrew-shaped flagellum appears at one pole and rotates like a propeller (it does not wave), moving the whole bacterium across a schematic water field. Labels say often or sometimes.
scenes.narration: Many bacteria also have a cell wall that helps prevent bursting when water enters. Some have a capsule outside. Some have flagella that spin to push them through water. These parts vary, but the working cell remains.

scenes.tts: Now open the virus. Its D N A or R N A sits inside a protein capsid. Some viruses add a lipid envelope outside. There is no cytoplasm and no ribosome workbench. A host cell must build every viral protein.
scenes.caption: Now open the virus. Its DNA or RNA sits inside a protein capsid. Some viruses add a lipid envelope outside. There is no cytoplasm and no ribosome workbench. A host cell must build every viral protein.
scenes.visual: The bacterium shifts left but keeps moving. The blue virus enlarges at right. A blue capsid separates around a purple block labeled DNA or RNA. A pink outer ring appears with the label envelope, some viruses. Empty interior labels read no cytoplasm and no ribosomes.
scenes.narration: Now open the virus. Its DNA or RNA sits inside a protein capsid. Some viruses add a lipid envelope outside. There is no cytoplasm and no ribosome workbench. A host cell must build every viral protein.

scenes.tts: Genes are the shared part, not proof that both are cells. The bacterium reads its genes with its own ribosomes. Viral genes can be read only after they reach a suitable host cell.
scenes.visual: Purple genes blocks align between the two objects. On the bacterium side, the block feeds directly into moving ribosome workbenches. On the virus side, the path stops at a gap, then continues through a dotted arrow toward the pink host cell.
scenes.narration: Genes are the shared part, not proof that both are cells. The bacterium reads its genes with its own ribosomes. Viral genes can be read only after they reach a suitable host cell.

scenes.tts: A working cell also needs energy and carbon. Energy powers the work. Carbon supplies material for new parts. For a useful first model, sort bacteria into common patterns by where those inputs come from.
scenes.visual: Keep the green bacterium centered. Two gold lanes enter it: energy on top and carbon below. The lanes split into three curved routes while the bacterium's membrane and ribosomes continue moving. Header: three common patterns.
scenes.narration: A working cell also needs energy and carbon. Energy powers the work. Carbon supplies material for new parts. For a useful first model, sort bacteria into common patterns by where those inputs come from.

scenes.tts: Heterotrophs take in carbon compounds for both energy and carbon. Photoautotrophs use light for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon. Chemoautotrophs use chemicals for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon.
scenes.visual: Transform the same two input lanes through three labeled settings, never a list of static cards. Food blocks feed both lanes for heterotroph. A moving light beam feeds energy for photoautotroph. A sulfur-compound block feeds energy for chemoautotroph. Carbon dioxide blocks feed both autotroph carbon lanes.
scenes.narration: Heterotrophs take in carbon compounds for both energy and carbon. Photoautotrophs use light for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon. Chemoautotrophs use chemicals for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon.

scenes.tts: Predict the pattern in a dark spring. The bacterium uses sulfur compounds for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon. Which name fits, and which input tells you?
scenes.visual: The scene becomes a dark schematic spring. No light beam appears. Sulfur-compound blocks enter the energy lane; carbon dioxide enters the carbon lane. Three names orbit slowly: heterotroph, photoautotroph, chemoautotroph. Large on-screen word: PREDICT.
scenes.narration: Predict the pattern in a dark spring. The bacterium uses sulfur compounds for energy and carbon dioxide for carbon. Which name fits, and which input tells you?

scenes.visual: Hold the dark spring and question. Sulfur and carbon dioxide blocks continue drifting toward the bacterium, but no name is selected.

scenes.tts: Chemoautotroph fits. Chemical energy selects chemo, and carbon dioxide supplies the carbon. The model is a simplification. Energy source and carbon source are separate questions, and a few bacteria mix the patterns.
scenes.visual: Chemoautotroph locks above the bacterium. The word splits into CHEMO over the sulfur energy lane and AUTOTROPH over the carbon-dioxide lane. Then the lanes separate visibly under the note useful simplification; a few faint crossed routes show mixed patterns without naming them.
scenes.narration: Chemoautotroph fits. Chemical energy selects chemo, and carbon dioxide supplies the carbon. The model is a simplification. Energy source and carbon source are separate questions, and a few bacteria mix the patterns.

scenes.tts: Dependence alone does not make a cell nonliving. Some bacteria grow only inside other cells, yet keep ribosomes and metabolism. Viruses remain different because they are not cells and have no ribosomes of their own.
scenes.visual: A small green bacterium enters the pink host cell while keeping its own membrane and moving ribosomes. Beside it, the blue virus still routes its purple genes to the host's ribosomes. Labels: dependent cell and noncellular virus.
scenes.narration: Dependence alone does not make a cell nonliving. Some bacteria grow only inside other cells, yet keep ribosomes and metabolism. Viruses remain different because they are not cells and have no ribosomes of their own.

scenes.tts: Size does not decide the case either. Most viruses are smaller than typical bacteria. But some giant viruses are longer than small bacteria, so that shortcut breaks. Parts and work matter more than length.
scenes.visual: A horizontal schematic size track appears without spoken numbers. A typical blue virus and green bacterium slide to their usual order. Then a giant blue virus passes a small green bacterium. The label size test cracks; parts plus work remains bright.
scenes.narration: Size does not decide the case either. Most viruses are smaller than typical bacteria. But some giant viruses are longer than small bacteria, so that shortcut breaks. Parts and work matter more than length.

scenes.tts: The comparison now has a reason. Bacterial parts let the cell obtain inputs and build proteins. Viral parts carry genes between hosts. Bacteria are living cells; viruses are not cells and are classed nonliving.
scenes.visual: Reassemble the carried world. The green bacterium takes in gold inputs and runs its ribosomes. The blue virus carries its purple genes toward the pink host. Two arrows converge on the words parts explain the difference.
scenes.narration: The comparison now has a reason. Bacterial parts let the cell obtain inputs and build proteins. Viral parts carry genes between hosts. Bacteria are living cells; viruses are not cells and are classed nonliving.

scenes.visual: End card shows one line only: 'Bacteria are living cells; viruses are not cells and are classed nonliving.' No subtitle, URL, title, or smaller line. Gentle green and blue ambient motion continues behind the text.
